lessons.title: Copilot and agent capabilities
lessons.summary: Compare Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Researcher, Analyst, custom agents, and monthly versus pay-as-you-go models.
learningObjectives: Compare Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Researcher, and Analyst
Describe how custom agents extend Microsoft 365 Copilot experiences
Distinguish monthly licenses from pay-as-you-go agent usage
Choose the Copilot or agent capability for a business scenario
lessons.explanation: Relecloud Marketing compares Copilot experiences. Microsoft Copilot Chat is a managed chat experience. Microsoft 365 Copilot capabilities add licensed work-context experiences in Microsoft 365 apps and services, respecting permissions and policies. Agents are focused AI experiences for a task, process, or knowledge source; they can come from Microsoft, the organization, or third parties. Researcher supports research and synthesis scenarios. Analyst supports data analysis-style work. Administrators compare monthly per-user Copilot licensing with pay-as-you-go scenarios, including SharePoint-related consumption, without memorizing prices. Admins ask who needs the capability, which settings can be enabled or disabled, what billing policy applies, and how usage will be monitored.

terminology.definition: A managed chat experience for organizational users.
Licensed work-context Copilot capabilities in Microsoft 365.
A focused AI experience for a task or knowledge source.
A capability for research and synthesis.
A capability for data analysis-style tasks.

lessons.businessScenario: Relecloud Marketing is planning a product launch. Nia wants everyday chat, Priya wants work-context help in Word and Teams, and Alex wants a launch FAQ agent grounded in approved campaign material.
lessons.technicalExample: Capability picker: `Brainstorm tagline=Copilot Chat`; `Summarize Teams decisions=licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot`; `Analyze campaign data=Analyst`; `Research market themes=Researcher`; `Answer launch FAQ=custom agent`.

misconception.myth: Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Researcher, Analyst, and agents are interchangeable names for one feature.
misconception.reality: They represent different experiences, licensing and billing considerations, data context, and governance decisions.

lessons.examTakeaway: Choose by job: general chat for everyday prompts, licensed Copilot for Microsoft 365 work context, Researcher for synthesis, Analyst for data reasoning, and custom agents for a focused process or knowledge source.
lessons.recap: Compare Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Researcher, Analyst, custom agents, and monthly versus pay-as-you-go models.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of a newsroom: Copilot Chat is the whiteboard, Microsoft 365 Copilot is the editor with access to approved drafts, Researcher is the librarian, Analyst is the data desk, and an agent is a beat-specific assistant.
lessons.anotherExample: Litware uses Copilot Chat for first drafts, Microsoft 365 Copilot for meeting and document workflows, Analyst for survey patterns, and a partner-policy agent for sellers.

lessons.title: Basic Copilot administration
lessons.summary: Assign Copilot licenses, configure settings, monitor billing policies, review usage and adoption, and manage prompts.
learningObjectives: Describe how admins assign Copilot licenses and configure tenant settings
Identify billing policies, usage reports, and adoption insights for Copilot
Explain how prompt management supports responsible Copilot use
Order steps for a basic Copilot pilot rollout
lessons.explanation: Basic Copilot administration begins with scope. Decide pilot users, assign licenses directly or through groups, and review Copilot settings in the Microsoft 365 admin center. The existing 'Assign Microsoft Copilot licenses for a Sales pilot' lab gives hands-on practice with license assignment, settings, and usage reporting. Admins also monitor pay-as-you-go billing policies where used, review Copilot usage and adoption through Copilot Analytics and Microsoft 365 admin center reports, and manage prompts such as saving, sharing, scheduling, and deleting. The goal is a governed rollout, not a surprise tenant-wide enablement.

terminology.definition: An entitlement assigned to enable licensed Copilot capabilities.
Using group membership to manage license assignment.
Admin controls for available Copilot experiences.
A report used to monitor adoption.
Saving, sharing, scheduling, and deleting prompts.

lessons.businessScenario: Relecloud starts with a Sales pilot. Nia must assign licenses to the pilot group, review Copilot settings, monitor adoption, and make sure prompt sharing does not become an unmanaged shortcut.
lessons.technicalExample: Pilot checklist: `Group=Sales-Copilot-Pilot`; `Assignment=Copilot licenses via group`; `Settings=review admin center controls`; `Reports=usage and adoption after two weeks`; `Prompt governance=owner and sharing review`.

misconception.myth: Assigning a Copilot license is the entire rollout plan.
misconception.reality: Licensing enables eligible experiences, but admins still manage settings, billing policies, reports, adoption, and prompt lifecycle.

lessons.examTakeaway: For Copilot admin scenarios, look for the lifecycle: scope users, assign licenses, configure settings, manage pay-as-you-go policies where used, monitor usage/adoption, and govern prompts.
lessons.recap: Assign Copilot licenses, configure settings, monitor billing policies, review usage and adoption, and manage prompts.
lessons.simplerExplanation: A Copilot rollout is like lending demo equipment: licenses are the checkout tags, settings are the operating rules, usage reports are the sign-out sheet, billing policies are spending limits, and prompt governance is the shared instruction binder.
lessons.anotherExample: Contoso practises the Sales pilot in the course lab, fixes a missing usage location, assigns licenses to the pilot group, reviews Copilot settings, and opens the usage report before expanding.

lessons.title: Basic agent administration
lessons.summary: Manage agent inventory, user access, creation, approval, blocking, sharing, ownership, usage, operational insights, and lifecycle.
learningObjectives: Identify agent inventory details such as owner, sharing, usage, and status
Describe controls for agent creation, approval, blocking, and user access
Explain how operational insights support agent lifecycle management
Choose admin actions for risky or unmanaged agents
lessons.explanation: Basic agent administration keeps agents useful and safe. Admins use agent inventory or registry views to review agents, owners, source, status, usage, and lifecycle signals. They configure user access to agents, create or review agents, approve or reject requests, block risky agents, and manage sharing and ownership. The existing 'Manage Microsoft 365 Copilot agent inventory' lab practises publishing an approved agent to Sales, blocking a risky third-party agent, setting allowed categories, limiting sharing, and viewing usage. Monitoring may involve the Microsoft 365 admin center and Microsoft Power Platform admin center, so UI details should be verified often.

terminology.definition: An admin view of agents and governance details.
A process to approve, reject, update, or publish agents.
Restricting an agent that should not be used.
Controls for who can discover or use an agent.

lessons.businessScenario: Relecloud's agent list contains a polished Sales FAQ agent, a broad third-party research agent, and an abandoned demo agent. Alex must decide what to approve, restrict, own, monitor, or retire.
lessons.technicalExample: Agent inventory row: `Agent=Sales FAQ`; `Source=org-built`; `Owner=Sales Enablement`; `Audience=Sales pilot`; `Status=pending approval`; `Action=publish to scoped users`; `Follow-up=usage and lifecycle review`.

misconception.myth: After an agent is created, ownership and sharing no longer matter.
misconception.reality: Agents need accountable owners, scoped availability, approval decisions, blocking when necessary, monitoring, and lifecycle review.

lessons.examTakeaway: Agent admin questions usually turn on governance verbs: inventory, configure user access, create or review, approve, reject, block, share, assign owner, monitor usage, and manage lifecycle.
lessons.recap: Manage agent inventory, user access, creation, approval, blocking, sharing, ownership, usage, operational insights, and lifecycle.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Agents are like self-service kiosks in a store. Inventory tells you which kiosks exist, approval decides which open, sharing controls who can use them, ownership says who fixes them, and monitoring shows whether they should stay.
lessons.anotherExample: Wide World Importers approves a Procurement FAQ agent only for buyers, blocks an unreviewed vendor agent, and retires a test agent that has no owner or usage.
